1. Executive Legislative Architecture and Statutory Foundations
1.1 Dual-Mechanism Statutory Design under the Income Tax Act

Canada's primary fiscal instrument for stimulating industrial research and experimental innovation is the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, which represents the largest single source of federal government support for business-led research and development, with over $13.7 billion in expenditures claimed and $3.9 billion in tax credits delivered annually1. Administered jointly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and the Department of Finance Canada, the program is codified within the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR)1. Rather than operating as a discretionary grant or a single-stage deduction, the federal SR&ED regime functions through a distinct, two-stage statutory mechanism that separates the timing of income tax deductions from the generation of dollar-for-dollar tax credits1.

The first statutory pillar is codified in Section 37 of the ITA, which establishes the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures1. Under Subsection 37(1) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada may deduct qualifying current expenditures—and, following legislative amendments effective after December 15, 2024, qualifying capital expenditures—incurred in Canada for SR&ED directly against net income for tax purposes in the taxation year in which the expenditures are incurred1. Because the subsection 37(1) mechanism operates as an open-ended expenditure pool rather than a decaying annual deduction, any portion of the pool not deducted in the current taxation year may be carried forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years, subject only to loss restriction event rules under Subsection 37(6.1) and Paragraph 37(1)(h) of the ITA upon an acquisition of control1. While Subsection 37(1) governs SR&ED carried on inside Canada, Subsection 37(2) of the ITA provides a parallel current deduction for permissible SR&ED expenditures incurred outside Canada, and Subsection 37(8) of the ITA sets forth the interpretive rules determining which expenditures qualify under each territorial stream1.

The second statutory pillar is codified in Section 127 and Section 127.1 of the ITA, which govern the calculation, application, and refundability of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (ITCs)1. Once a claimant computes its allowable SR&ED expenditure pool under section 37 and adjusts that base for prescribed proxy amounts, government and non-government assistance, and third-party payment limitations to arrive at its "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" as defined in Subsection 127(9) of the ITA, the claimant earns an ITC that directly offsets Part I federal tax otherwise payable under Subsection 127(5) of the ITA2. Depending on the legal status, ownership structure, taxable capital, and gross revenue of the claimant, unused ITCs are either refunded in cash pursuant to Section 127.1 of the ITA or carried back three taxation years and forward up to twenty taxation years to reduce Part I tax in other periods1. Crucially, any federal SR&ED ITC claimed as an offset against Part I tax or received as a cash refund is recaptured into the tax base by reducing the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the subsequent taxation year (or being included in taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(t) of the ITA if the pool goes negative), thereby preventing a double fiscal benefit on the same dollar of expenditure11.

body.text: 1.2 The 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms: From Budget 2024 and the Fall Economic Statement to Bill C-15

Between 2024 and 2026, the federal SR&ED regime underwent its most significant structural overhaul since the 2012–2014 legislative retrenchments8. For over a decade following the 2012 federal budget, the SR&ED program operated under tightened fiscal parameters: capital expenditures and capital lease costs were excluded effective January 1, 2014; the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) rate was reduced from 65% (for 2012 and prior years) to 60% in 2013 and 55% from 2014 onward; arm's-length contractor payments were restricted to an 80% inclusion rate; and the enhanced 35% refundable credit remained strictly confined to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) up to a static $3 million expenditure limit2.

Recognizing a sustained decline in Canadian business enterprise R&D (BERD) intensity relative to Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) peers, the Department of Finance initiated a two-phase policy review in early 20242. The initial consultation, which concluded on April 15, 2024, explored cost-neutral modernization options2. However, in Budget 2024 (tabled April 16, 2024), the federal government abandoned the cost-neutral constraint, committing an initial $600 million over four years and launching a second-phase consultation on April 25, 2024 (with stakeholder submissions closing on May 27, 2024) alongside parallel consultations on a Canadian patent box regime and an immediate 100% accelerated Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) for patents and rights to use patented information acquired on or after April 16, 2024 and becoming available for use prior to 2027 (with property becoming available for use during 2027 continuing to benefit from the Accelerated Investment Incentive)2.

The subsequent legislative reform evolved through two distinct fiscal stages between December 2024 and March 2026, creating a critical audit verification distinction between interim proposals and final enacted law1. In the first stage, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (tabled December 16, 2024)—and subsequently detailed in draft legislative and explanatory notes released in August 2025—proposed four foundational reforms intended to apply to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (that is, after December 15, 2024)1. Those interim proposals comprised increasing the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced credit from $3 million to $4.5 million, expanding the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the historical $10 million to $50 million range to a wider $15 million to $75 million range, extending eligibility for the 35% refundable credit to "Eligible Canadian Public Corporations" (ECPCs), and restoring the eligibility of capital expenditures and shared-use equipment for both the subsection 37(1) deduction and the section 127 ITC, with partial refundability set at 40%1.

In the second and definitive legislative stage, Budget 2025 (tabled November 4, 2025) and its implementing legislation, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, expanded the expenditure limit even further, superseding the interim $4.5 million FES proposal and enacting a $6 million annual expenditure limit retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 20248. Under the enacted Bill C-15 statutory framework, qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs can earn the enhanced 35% refundable ITC on up to $6 million of qualified SR&ED expenditures annually—generating up to $2.1 million in refundable federal tax credits per year, double the historical $1.05 million ceiling8.

body.text: 1.3 Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and CCPC Threshold Mechanics

Historically, the requirement that a claimant be a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) throughout the taxation year to access the 35% refundable credit created a severe structural distortion in Canadian capital markets2. When a domestic technology, clean-tech, or life sciences startup completed an initial public offering (IPO) on the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX), TSX Venture Exchange, NYSE, or NASDAQ, or accepted a controlling equity investment from non-resident venture capital funds, it immediately ceased to be a CCPC, triggering a deemed taxation year-end under the ITA3. Upon losing CCPC status, the corporation's SR&ED ITC rate dropped abruptly from 35% to 15%, and—even more consequentially for pre-profit scaling enterprises—its credits became entirely non-refundable2. Simultaneously, anti-avoidance rules governing "substantive CCPCs" enacted in 2024 targeted private corporations that manipulated technical corporate status to avoid investment income taxation without granting them CCPC R&D incentives27.

To eliminate the tax penalty on domestic public listings while preserving Canadian ownership requirements, the amended Subsection 127(10.1) and Subsection 127(9) of the ITA introduced the Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) category for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 20241. A corporation qualifies as an ECPC throughout a taxation year only if it satisfies three cumulative statutory conditions29. First, with respect to residency, the corporation must be a taxable Canadian corporation that is resident in Canada throughout the taxation year29. Second, with respect to corporate status, the corporation must have a class of shares of its capital stock listed on a designated stock exchange in Canada or abroad (such as the TSX, NYSE, or NASDAQ), or have validly elected or been designated by the Minister to be a public corporation under subsection 89(1) of the ITA, and therefore not be a CCPC29. Third, with respect to control, the corporation must not be controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever (encompassing both de jure voting control and de facto control under subsection 256(5.1) of the ITA) by one or more non-resident persons30.

In addition, under the definitions in Subsection 127(9) of the ITA, an "eligible subsidiary" that is resident in Canada and has not less than 90% of the issued shares of each class of its capital stock owned, directly or indirectly, by one or more corporations that are ECPCs is similarly integrated into the ECPC framework9. This legislative architecture ensures that Canadian-headquartered, widely held public innovators and their 90%-owned domestic operating subsidiaries retain access to the 35% refundable credit on up to $6 million of current SR&ED expenditures during their capital-intensive growth stages, while foreign-controlled multinational subsidiaries remain in the 15% non-refundable basic tier9.
2. Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, and Carryover Rules
2.1 Enhanced 35% vs. Basic 15% Investment Tax Credit Tiers

The federal SR&ED program operates a dual-rate volume-based credit architecture under Subsections 127(9) and 127(10.1) of the ITA1. Under Paragraph (a.1) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in Subsection 127(9) of the ITA, the baseline federal SR&ED ITC rate is 15% of the amount by which a taxpayer's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at the end of the taxation year exceeds the total of all amounts each of which is a super-allowance benefit amount for the year in respect of a province9. This 15% basic rate applies to all corporations that are neither CCPCs nor ECPCs (such as foreign-controlled private corporations and large public corporations exceeding the revenue phase-out), to CCPCs and ECPCs on their qualified SR&ED expenditures in excess of their annual expenditure limit, and to unincorporated claimants including sole proprietorships, individuals, partnerships, and trusts10.

Conversely, under Subsection 127(10.1) of the ITA, a corporation that is a CCPC or an ECPC throughout the taxation year is entitled to an additional 20% ITC on the lesser of its SR&ED qualified expenditure pool and its annual expenditure limit for the taxation year1. When combined with the 15% basic ITC under subsection 127(9), qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earn a total 35% enhanced ITC on up to $6 million of qualified SR&ED expenditures per taxation year1.

For partnerships conducting SR&ED, a partnership is not a separate taxpayer under the ITA; instead, under Subsection 127(8) of the ITA, the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool and the resulting 15% basic ITC are computed at the partnership level as if the partnership were a person and its fiscal period were its taxation year, and are then allocated to the members of the partnership at the end of the fiscal period3. However, partnership ITC allocations are strictly constrained: limited partners and "specified members" (passive partners defined in subsection 248(1)) are restricted by the at-risk rules (further reduced by clean economy tax credit allocations under subsection 127.47(1)) and Subsection 127(8.2) of the ITA, and a partnership cannot earn the 35% enhanced CCPC rate directly9.
2.2 Phase-Out Formulas: Taxable Capital Employed in Canada and Average Gross Revenue

The $6 million baseline expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC is not a flat entitlement for all CCPCs and ECPCs; it is subject to mandatory sharing among associated corporations under Subsections 127(10.3) and 127(10.4) of the ITA, proration for short taxation years of less than 51 weeks, and a statutory phase-out ("grind") based on corporate size in the preceding taxation year3. Ignoring the association rules in section 256 of the ITA—or failing to file a formal expenditure limit allocation agreement under subsection 127(10.3) before group members file their claims—is a frequent compliance error that leads to immediate reassessment when an associated corporate group collectively claims more than $6 million at the enhanced rate8.

Following the enactment of Bill C-15 in March 2026 (effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024), the expenditure limit phase-out rules were expanded into the taxable capital and gross revenue phase-out formulas under Subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.6) of the ITA1. For a CCPC and its associated corporations under Subsection 127(10.2) of the ITA, the $6 million expenditure limit begins to phase out on a straight-line basis when the associated group's taxable capital employed in Canada (determined under Part I.3 of the ITA, sections 181.2 to 181.4, or notional large corporations tax rules) for the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds $15 million, and is reduced to nil when prior-year taxable capital reaches $75 million (expanded from the historical $10 million to $50 million band; the former prior-year taxable income component of the CCPC phase-out had already been eliminated for taxation years ending on or after March 19, 2019)3. Expressed mathematically, for a CCPC with prior-year associated taxable capital (TC) between $15 million and $75 million, the annual expenditure limit (EL) is calculated as: EL = $6 million × [($60 million − (TC − $15 million)) ÷ $60 million].

Under this linear formula, for every $10 of taxable capital employed in Canada above $15 million, the corporation's $6 million expenditure limit is reduced by $117. Importantly, CCPCs are also permitted under the reformed rules to elect to utilize the gross-revenue-based phase-out structure instead of taxable capital where high balance-sheet capital (such as debt or preferred equity raised for pre-revenue R&D) would otherwise prematurely eliminate their expenditure limit11.

Because public corporations frequently raise substantial equity capital on public markets that inflates Part I.3 taxable capital well before achieving commercial scale, Subsection 127(10.6) of the ITA determines an ECPC's expenditure limit using average gross revenue rather than taxable capital1. Average gross revenue is calculated over the three preceding fiscal years as reported in the consolidated financial statements of the ECPC (or the single economic entity group, as defined in subsection 127(9) where the assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and cash flows of group members are presented as those of a single economic entity)1. The $6 million expenditure limit is available in full where average annual gross revenue (GR) does not exceed $15 million, phases out linearly between $15 million and $75 million, and reaches nil at $75 million11: EL = $6 million × [($60 million − (GR − $15 million)) ÷ $60 million].
2.3 Refundability Matrix, Carryback, Carryforward, and Change-of-Control Restrictions

Whether an earned SR&ED ITC yields an immediate cash refund from the Receiver General or remains a non-refundable tax offset depends on Section 127.1 of the ITA (specifically subsections 127.1(2) and 127.1(2.01)) and the distinction between current and capital expenditures1. Under Subsection 127.1(2) and Subsection 127.1(2.01) of the ITA, the 35% enhanced ITC earned by a qualifying CCPC (including a CCPC that is neither a qualifying corporation nor an excluded corporation) or an ECPC on qualified SR&ED expenditures of a current nature up to its $6 million expenditure limit is 100% refundable1. Conversely, for depreciable capital property acquired after December 15, 2024, the 35% enhanced ITC earned by a qualifying CCPC or ECPC within its expenditure limit is 40% refundable, rendering an effective immediate cash refund of 14.0% (35% × 40%) of the capital cost, while the remaining 60% of the ITC (21.0% of the capital cost) is available to offset Part I tax payable or be carried over1.

When a CCPC incurs qualified SR&ED expenditures exceeding its $6 million expenditure limit, those excess expenditures earn the basic 15% ITC2. If the CCPC meets the definition of a "qualifying corporation" under Subsection 127.1(2) of the ITA—meaning its prior-year taxable income (combined with associated corporations) does not exceed its "qualifying income limit" (which starts at $500,000 and phases out as prior-year associated taxable capital passes $15 million)—then 40% of the 15% ITC earned on those excess expenditures is refundable (an effective 6.0% cash refund)13. If the CCPC exceeds the qualifying income or capital thresholds, the 15% ITC on expenditures above the limit is entirely non-refundable17. Similarly, unincorporated individuals and certain trusts earn the basic 15% ITC, of which 40% is refundable against current and capital SR&ED expenditures after offsetting Part I tax payable, whereas foreign-controlled corporations, public corporations with average gross revenue of $75 million or more, and other non-qualifying corporations earn the 15% basic ITC with 0% refundability2.

body.text: Any non-refundable ITC (or the non-refundable portion of a partially refundable ITC) that is not absorbed by Part I tax payable in the taxation year earned may be carried back up to 3 taxation years to recover prior Part I taxes paid, or carried forward up to 20 taxation years under Subsection 127(9) of the ITA (the carryforward period having been extended from 10 to 20 years by the May 2, 2006 federal budget for taxation years ending after 2005)3. However, if a corporation undergoes a "loss restriction event" (an acquisition of control by a person or group of persons), Subsection 37(6.1) and Paragraph 37(1)(h) of the ITA (alongside subsections 127(9.1) and 127(9.2) for ITCs) stream the corporation's unused section 37 SR&ED deduction pool and unused ITC carryforwards1. Post-acquisition utilization of those pools is strictly prohibited unless the corporation continues to carry on the specific business in which the SR&ED expenditures were incurred for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only to the extent of income from that same or a similar business1.
3. Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs) and Overhead Calculation Methodologies
3.1 Direct Labour, Specified Employee Caps, and 2026 YMPE Benchmarks

Salaries and wages represent the largest expenditure component of most Canadian SR&ED claims3. To qualify under Paragraph 37(1)(a) of the ITA and Section 2900 of the ITR, salary or wages must be incurred in respect of employees who are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada3. The CRA classifies an employee's duties based on technical function rather than job title, encompassing hands-on experimentation, engineering design, prototype fabrication, scientific testing, and direct first-line technical supervision of SR&ED personnel, plus eligible "directly-related" support work (under subsection 248(1)(d)) where that work is commensurate with the needs of the core SR&ED activities6. Administrative, clerical, legal, marketing, and executive management activities that do not constitute direct technical participation are excluded from direct SR&ED labour (Line 300 of Form T661), though certain indirect support costs may be captured through overhead3. Furthermore, under section 78 of the ITA, unpaid accrued salaries or wages that are not actually paid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in the taxation year and may only be claimed in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid.

The Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose stringent anti-avoidance caps on the salaries and wages of "specified employees"—commonly affecting startup founders, owner-managers, and family members3. Under Subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a "specified employee" is an employee who is a "specified shareholder" of the employer corporation (meaning a person who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or of any related corporation, counting shares owned by persons with whom the taxpayer does not deal at arm's length) or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer13.

For any specified employee, four cumulative statutory restrictions apply simultaneously across the direct labour pool and the overhead proxy calculation8. First, all bonuses, performance incentives, stock option benefits (under section 7 of the ITA), and any remuneration based on profits are strictly disallowed as SR&ED expenditures for a specified employee8. Second, under Subsection 37(9.1) of the ITA, the maximum amount of direct SR&ED salary or wages of a specified employee that can be included in the subsection 37(1) SR&ED deduction pool and claimed for ITCs is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual was a specified employee; furthermore, under Subsection 37(9.3) of the ITA, if the specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, this 5 × YMPE limit must be allocated among the associated corporations using a prescribed agreement (Form T1174)13. Third, under Subsection 2900(7) of the ITR, when the claimant elects the Proxy Method to compute overhead, the amount of a specified employee's salary that can enter the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) salary base (Line 502 of Form T661) cannot exceed 75% of the employee's total salary or wages for the year (excluding bonuses and taxable benefits)3. Fourth, under Subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the ITR, even where 75% of the specified employee's salary is higher, the specified employee's inclusion in the PPA salary base is further capped at 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days the individual is employed by the taxpayer in the year8.

For the 2026 taxation year, the statutory CPP Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) is $74,600.00 (with a Year's Basic Exemption of $3,500.00, an employer and employee first-band CPP contribution rate of 5.95% outside Quebec, and a maximum first-band CPP contribution of $4,230.45 per employee and employer)13. body.text: 3.2 Overhead Calculation: The 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) vs. Traditional Method

In Part 3, Section A of Form T661, a claimant must elect annually between two mutually exclusive methodologies for calculating SR&ED overhead and other expenditures: the Proxy Method (Line 160) or the Traditional Method (Line 162)3. Once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the choice of method is irrevocable for that taxation year17.

Under the Proxy Method (elected under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the ITA within the time set by Subsection 37(10) of the ITA, and computed under Section 2900 of the ITR), the taxpayer does not identify, track, or claim actual SR&ED overhead expenditures on Form T6613. Instead, the taxpayer computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base (Line 502) under Subsection 2900(4) of the ITR3. A widespread error in some technical literature is citing a 65% proxy rate; in fact, the PPA rate was 65% only for taxation years ending in 2012 and prior, transitioned to 60% for 2013, and has been fixed at 55% since January 1, 20148. Overstating the PPA at 65% overstates the proxy overhead by 10 percentage points and results in automatic downward adjustment upon CRA assessment8.

Furthermore, three technical rules govern the PPA calculation under the Proxy Method3. First, the PPA salary base (Part 5, Line 502) is narrower than gross payroll: it includes only the base salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, meaning that even for regular arm's-length employees (whose bonuses and taxable benefits are allowable as direct SR&ED labour on Line 300), bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and employer-paid statutory payroll deductions (CPP, EI, EHT, WCB) are excluded from the Line 502 PPA salary base3. Second, under Subsection 2900(6) of the ITR, the PPA is subject to an overall non-SR&ED expense ceiling and cannot exceed the claimant's total business deductions for the year net of SR&ED deductions and specific statutory exclusions, preventing shell entities with no actual overhead from generating notional tax credits4. Third, because the PPA is a notional statutory construct, it is treated as a qualified expenditure solely for Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculation purposes in Part 4 of Form T661 and is never added to the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, the actual underlying overhead expenses (such as office rent, utilities, human resources, and general supplies) remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under section 9 and paragraph 18(1)(a) of the ITA3.

Under the Traditional Method, the taxpayer enters "0" on Lines 355 and 502, leaves Part 5 blank, and claims actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T6613. To qualify under the Traditional Method, every claimed overhead expenditure must be directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—meaning the cost would not have been incurred had the SR&ED not been carried out3. Unlike the PPA, eligible overhead under the Traditional Method is added directly to the subsection 37(1) SR&ED deduction pool and qualifies for ITCs3.
3.3 Cloud Computing, Software Subscriptions, and Materials Consumed or Transformed

A major compliance pitfall for software, artificial intelligence, data analytics, and product design claimants involves the treatment of cloud computing costs (such as AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud GPU clusters) and specialized software or CAD subscriptions8. Under CRA administrative policy and the structure of Section 2900 of the ITR, if a claimant elects the Proxy Method, cloud computing invoices, hosting environments, and software or CAD subscription fees cannot be claimed separately8. Because the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount under Regulation 2900(4) stands in for all overhead and indirect infrastructure costs of every kind, claiming cloud computing or software subscriptions alongside the 55% proxy constitutes double-counting and is systematically disallowed on audit8. Conversely, if a claimant incurs massive, verifiable incremental compute costs (such as training foundation AI models or running large-scale engineering simulations on leased cloud clusters) that exceed 55% of its direct SR&ED salary base, the claimant must deliberately elect the Traditional Method (Line 162) and maintain granular, contemporaneous usage logs proving that the cloud instances were directly related and incremental to the eligible SR&ED projects8.

With respect to materials, Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) of the ITA and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy distinguish between materials consumed—which are rendered virtually valueless or destroyed as a result of the prosecution of SR&ED (such as chemical reagents, biological media, or destructive testing coupons)—and materials transformed, which are integrated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or custom test rig during the SR&ED process8. Both consumed and transformed materials are 100% includable in the subsection 37(1) deduction pool and 100% eligible for ITCs under either the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method3. However, if an experimental prototype or transformed material is subsequently sold commercially or converted to commercial use, Recapture of SR&ED ITCs applies under Subsections 127(27) to 127(35) of the ITA, requiring the claimant to add to its Part I tax payable, in the year of sale or conversion, the lesser of the ITC originally earned on the property and the amount obtained by applying the ITC rate to the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value at conversion)3.
3.4 Arm's-Length Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Transfers, and Look-Through Rules

When a claimant contracts out SR&ED work to third-party subcontractors or research institutions, the statutory treatment depends on whether the contractor deals at arm's length with the claimant and where the work is performed8. Under Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.01) to (iii) of the ITA, contract payments qualify only if the SR&ED is performed in Canada on behalf of the claimant (or represents eligible third-party payments to approved Canadian universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit SR&ED corporations)3. Payments to foreign subcontractors performing work outside Canada are ineligible for SR&ED ITCs (outside of the narrow rule in subsection 37(1.4), which deems salary or wages for SR&ED carried on outside Canada, capped under subsection 37(1.5) at 10% of the salary or wages for SR&ED carried on in Canada, to be expenditures for SR&ED carried on in Canada)1.

While 100% of an eligible arm's-length contract payment is deductible in computing income under Subsection 37(1) of the ITA, Subparagraph (a)(ii) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in Subsection 127(9) of the ITA restricts the amount entering the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes to 80% of the eligible contract expenditure8. This statutory 20% haircut was enacted to strip out the subcontractor's presumed profit margin from the federal tax credit base8. In addition, under the look-through rule formerly in Subsection 37(14) of the ITA (repealed by Bill C-15, S.C. 2026, c. 3, s. 5), a taxpayer claiming expenditures for SR&ED performed on its behalf by a third party had to look through the contract to ensure that the payment represents only underlying eligible expenditures of a current nature (excluding non-qualifying capital outlays such as buildings or land)1. Claimants must retain executed Statements of Work (SOWs), intellectual property ownership clauses confirming the work was performed on behalf of the claimant, and itemized invoices identifying the eligible technical activity9. Finally, if a claimant pays a non-arm's-length person (such as a sister corporation or subsidiary) to perform SR&ED, the payment itself is not a qualified expenditure to the payer; instead, the non-arm's-length performer incurs the underlying SR&ED costs directly and the parties may file a joint agreement under Subsection 127(13) of the ITA (Form T1146) to transfer the qualified expenditures from the performer to the payer3.
3.5 Restoration of Capital Expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE)

For a full decade (from January 1, 2014 to December 15, 2024), capital expenditures and capital lease costs were completely excluded from the SR&ED regime8. Under the legislative reforms introduced in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement and enacted via Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026), Paragraph 37(1)(b), Subsection 127(9), and Section 127.1 of the ITA were amended to restore the eligibility of capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024) that becomes available for use after that date1.

The restored capital regime establishes two distinct eligibility tracks depending on the intensity of SR&ED usage9. Under the first track, All or Substantially All (ASA) SR&ED Capital Property, depreciable tangible or intangible capital property (such as dedicated laboratory instrumentation, experimental tooling, moulds, pilot-scale machinery, and computers or software bought outright) qualifies at 100% of its capital cost for both the immediate deduction under paragraph 37(1)(b) and the ITC under subsection 127(9) if, at the time of acquisition, the property is intended either to use all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the performance of SR&ED in Canada, or to consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value in the performance of SR&ED in Canada1. Under the second track, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), where new machinery or equipment does not satisfy the 90% ASA test because it is used partly for commercial manufacturing and partly for R&D, but is used primarily (more than 50% of its operating time) for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, it qualifies as first-term shared-use-equipment and second-term shared-use-equipment under Subsection 127(9) of the ITA9. Shared-use equipment earns a partial credit on up to 50% of its capital cost, claimed in two equal instalments: 25% of the capital cost after the first period (minimum 12 months) and 25% after the second period (minimum 24 months)9.

Certain categories of capital property remain strictly ineligible: land, buildings, leasehold interests in buildings, inventory, and goodwill are statutorily excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures8. Moreover, while the August 2025 draft legislative notes referenced lease costs becoming payable on or after December 16, 20241, enacted compliance guidance under Bill C-15 cautions that equipment lease payments excluded since 2014 were not broadly restored in the same manner as outright capital acquisitions17. Finally, as detailed in Section 2.3, for CCPCs and ECPCs within the $6 million expenditure limit, the 35% enhanced ITC earned on eligible SR&ED capital expenditures is 40% refundable, compared to 100% refundability on current expenditures1.

body.text: 4. Scientific and Technological Eligibility Criteria and Judicial Precedents
4.1 Subsection 248(1) Definition: The "Why" and "How" Two-Pronged Framework and Statutory Exclusions

The legal threshold for whether a technical project qualifies for SR&ED tax incentives is governed exclusively by the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in Subsection 248(1) of the ITA6. The statute defines SR&ED as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls into one of three core categories, plus eligible support work6. Under Paragraph 248(1)(a), the definition encompasses basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view6. Under Paragraph 248(1)(b), it covers applied research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view6. Under Paragraph 248(1)(c), it covers experimental development—which accounts for over 95% of industrial SR&ED claims in Canada—defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto5. Finally, Paragraph 248(1)(d) includes eligible support work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer6.

In the CRA's consolidated administrative policy—Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives—the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) is operationalized through two overarching requirements known as the "Why" and the "How"6. The "Why" requirement mandates that the work be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement5. In a commercial or engineering context, this requires that the claimant encounter a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty—a system-level limitation, physical constraint, or algorithmic bottleneck whose resolution is not known or determinable on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge, standard practice, or routine engineering—and that the work seeks to generate new scientific or technological knowledge to overcome that uncertainty5. Commercial success or failure is legally irrelevant: a project that fails to achieve its business objective still satisfies the "Why" requirement if it generates technological advancement by proving why a hypothesized technical approach cannot function within specific boundary conditions5.

The "How" requirement mandates that the work be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis performed by qualified individuals6. Fulfilling the "How" requirement demands an iterative, structured scientific methodology: defining the underlying technological obstacle, formulating explicit technical hypotheses aimed at resolving the uncertainty, designing and executing experiments or rigorous mathematical and engineering analyses to test those hypotheses, observing and recording quantitative or qualitative results, and drawing logical conclusions as the work progresses5.

Conversely, Paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) of the ITA explicitly exclude eleven categories of commercial and routine technical activities from the definition of SR&ED, even when performed by highly qualified engineers or scientists5. Specifically, the statute excludes market research or sales promotion (paragraph (e)); quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes (paragraph (f)); research in the social sciences or the humanities (paragraph (g)); prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas (paragraph (h)); the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process (paragraph (i)); style changes (paragraph (j)); and routine data collection (paragraph (k))5.
4.2 Foundational Jurisprudence: Northwest Hydraulic, RIS-Christie, and C.W. Agencies

Canadian tax courts have developed a highly consistent body of jurisprudence interpreting subsection 248(1) of the ITA, anchored by three foundational decisions from the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal5. The cornerstone of Canadian SR&ED law is Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen , 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (Tax Court of Canada), in which Justice Donald Bowman (later Chief Justice of the Tax Court of Canada) articulated the five judicial criteria—universally referred to as the "Five Questions"—for determining whether a claimant's activities constitute SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the ITA5. First, Justice Bowman asked whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures, emphasizing that if the resolution of the problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures known to skilled practitioners in the field, no technological uncertainty exists5. Second, did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?5 Third, did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?5 Fourth, did the process result in a technological advancement, meaning an advancement in the general understanding of scientific relations or technology known to skilled practitioners, rather than merely building a commercial product?5 Fifth, was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept as the work progressed?5

Shortly after Northwest Hydraulic, the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen , [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132, 99 D.T.C. 5087 (FCA) (at paras. 10, 14–15) endorsed Justice Bowman's analytical framework while introducing a vital evidentiary clarification regarding the fifth criterion5. The Federal Court of Appeal held that while physical or digital contemporaneous documentation of test results is the most persuasive means of proving that repeatable scientific experimentation occurred, it is not strictly mandatory as a rule of substantive law that the evidence be solely documentary, and credible testimonial or secondary evidence may be presented to the Court5. Nevertheless, the Court cautioned that a taxpayer who fails to document testing steps as the work progresses assumes a heavy evidentiary risk that a reviewing auditor or trial judge will remain unpersuaded that a systematic investigation actually took place5.

Subsequently, in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen , 2001 FCA 393 (Federal Court of Appeal) (at para. 17), the Federal Court of Appeal formally synthesized and codified Justice Bowman's five Northwest Hydraulic criteria as the binding appellate standard across Canada5. The Court affirmed in C.W. Agencies that empirical trial-and-error tinkering lacks the requisite "total discipline of the scientific method" unless it is anchored by articulated hypotheses and systematic, documented progression from test to conclusion5.
4.3 Modern Audit and Litigation Precedents: National R&D Inc. (2020 TCC 65) and Tuna Temple Inc. (2026 FCA 175)

Recent jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal demonstrates how strictly Canadian courts police the boundary between routine commercial engineering or trial-and-error and genuine SR&ED5. In National R&D Inc. v. The Queen , 2020 TCC 65 (Docket 2017-3837(IT)G, July 7, 2020, per Justice Dominique Lafleur), the corporate appellant—an SR&ED consulting firm—appealed a November 3, 2014 assessment disallowing SR&ED credits for its 2011 taxation year (ended July 31, 2011) in respect of the "PTS Project," a computer program designed to automate time tracking and portions of filing SR&ED claims with the CRA5. At trial, the company's principal (Mr. Saini, who conducted the coding himself with the help of a student and was accepted by the Court as a "litigant expert" pursuant to Kaul v. The Queen) testified that existing web-based tools such as QuickBooks Online were in their infancy with limited functionality in 2011, and produced a "Project Timeline" alongside oral testimony regarding contemporaneous coding notes5. Justice Lafleur explicitly cited Northwest Hydraulic, RIS-Christie (paras. 14–15), C.W. Agencies (para. 17), and Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. (para. 94), acknowledging that testimonial evidence is legally acceptable even where documentary evidence is incomplete5. However, Justice Lafleur dismissed the appeal with costs to the Crown, holding (at paras. 67–75) that the witness's project timeline and testimony merely logged coding tasks and hours spent rather than demonstrating a "logical progression between each test and preceding or subsequent tests"5. Without evidence of structured hypothesis formulation, experimental validation, and causal progression between iterative tests, software development remains routine engineering rather than a systematic investigation5.

This stringent appellate standard was reinforced in Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada , 2026 FCA 175 (Federal Court of Appeal, 2026), in which the Federal Court of Appeal upheld the Tax Court's disallowance of thirteen fish-cutting and culinary recipe development projects40. Applying Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393), the Federal Court of Appeal held that even where a taxpayer provides credible oral testimony describing extensive practical experimentation and iterative adjustments, empirical trial-and-error aimed at commercial product optimization does not satisfy subsection 248(1) in the absence of genuine technological uncertainty, explicit hypothesis formulation under the scientific method, and systematic contemporaneous records of the hypotheses tested and results obtained40.

5.1 CRA Administrative Architecture and Form T661 Line-by-Line Anatomy

Unlike jurisdictions that require pre-approval or dual-ministry certification before R&D work commences, Canada's SR&ED program is self-assessed and administered post-facto by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) through specialized SR&ED Co-ordinating Tax Services Offices (CTSOs) across the country3. Within the CRA, every reviewed claim undergoes a bifurcated evaluation: Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs)—who are engineers or scientists in the relevant discipline—evaluate whether the claimed projects satisfy the technical eligibility requirements of subsection 248(1) of the ITA, while Financial Reviewers (FRs) audit the costing methodology, salary allocations, specified employee caps, contractor invoices, and ITC calculations under sections 37, 127, and 127.1 of the ITA3.

To access either the section 37 expenditure deduction or the section 127 ITC, a claimant must complete and file Form T661, Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim (in accordance with CRA Guide T4088, Guide to Form T661), together with Schedule T2SCH31 (Schedule 31), Investment Tax Credit – Corporations (for T2 corporate filers) or Form T2038(IND), Investment Tax Credit (Individuals) (for T1 individual or sole proprietorship filers)3. Since January 1, 2016, the CRA accepts only the consolidated T661(15) or subsequent current versions of Form T661, which is structured into ten distinct parts6:

body.text: 5.2 Claim Preparer Disclosure Requirements and Subsection 162(5.1) Joint-and-Several Penalties

A frequent technical error in outdated compliance summaries is misidentifying the location of the claim preparer disclosure on Form T661 as Part 7; on the current Form T661, Part 7 is Additional information, Part 8 is the Claim checklist, and Part 9 is Claim preparer information6. Under Paragraph 37(11)(b) and Subsection 162(5.1) of the ITA, every claimant must disclose in Part 9 whether a "claim preparer" (any person or partnership who accepts consideration to prepare, or assist in the preparation of, the SR&ED claim, excluding an employee of the claimant) was involved6.

Where an external consultant, accounting firm, or engineering advisor prepares or assists in preparing any portion of Form T661, Part 9 requires the claimant and the claim preparer to report the preparer's name, Business Number, billing arrangement code (specifically identifying contingency-fee percentages, flat fees, or hourly billing rates), and the total remuneration paid or payable6. If no external claim preparer was engaged, the claimant must still explicitly certify that fact by completing Lines 935, 970, and 975 in Part 96. If complete and accurate claim preparer information is omitted, missing, or misrepresented in Part 9, Subsection 162(5.1) of the ITA imposes a strict $1,000 penalty for each affected claim, for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally ("together or separately") liable20.

Furthermore, once the 18-month reporting deadline has passed, a claimant cannot add new projects, introduce omitted expenditure lines, or substitute alternative expenditures to replace amounts disallowed by the CRA during an audit7.

Critically, while Subsection 220(2.1) and Subsection 220(3.2) of the ITA generally grant the Minister of National Revenue discretionary authority under the Taxpayer Relief ("Fairness") provisions to waive filing requirements for prescribed forms or accept late-filed elections in cases of extraordinary circumstances or unintended mechanical errors, Subsection 220(2.2) of the ITA explicitly carves out SR&ED claims from ministerial relief17. Specifically, Subsection 220(2.2) of the ITA states that subsection 220(2.1) does not apply in respect of any prescribed form, receipt, document, or prescribed information that is filed with the Minister on or after the day specified in Subsection 37(11) or Paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in Subsection 127(9)23. Consequently, neither the CRA nor the Tax Court of Canada possesses any legal or equitable jurisdiction to extend a missed 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline, even by a single day8.
6. Provincial R&D Tax Credit Regimes, Direct Grants, and Federal Grind Mechanics

Every Canadian province (and the Yukon territory) except Prince Edward Island (which utilizes direct innovation grants) offers a provincial or territorial R&D tax incentive that piggybacks on the federal SR&ED definition in subsection 248(1) of the ITA12. While most provincial credits are administered directly by the CRA alongside the federal T2 return, Quebec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, Tax and Revenue Administration) operate autonomous corporate tax administrations with distinct forms and rules12.
6.1 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario conducting eligible SR&ED in the province have access to three complementary tax credits administered by the CRA12. The primary SME incentive is the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on T2 Schedule 566, which provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit (for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016; reduced from 10% prior to June 1, 2016) to CCPCs on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario12. The OITC applies up to an annual provincial expenditure limit of $3 million (yielding a maximum annual refundable OITC of $240,000), which must be shared among associated corporations and prorated for short taxation years19. Crucially, Ontario's $3 million OITC expenditure limit did not double when federal Bill C-15 increased the federal expenditure limit to $6 million32. Consequently, an Ontario CCPC spending $6 million on eligible current R&D earns the 8% OITC on its first $3 million, and 0% OITC on the band between $3 million and $6 million32. Furthermore, unlike the reformed federal SR&ED credit, the OITC covers only current expenditures and does not apply to the capital expenditures newly restored at the federal level19. The $3 million OITC expenditure limit phases out linearly when the associated group's prior-year taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25 million and $50 million12.

Complementing the OITC is the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on T2 Schedule 508, which provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016; reduced from 4.5%) available to all corporations (both CCPCs and non-CCPCs) with a permanent establishment in Ontario on eligible SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario, net of any OITC or OBRITC claimed12. Because the non-refundable ORDTC is treated as government assistance that immediately reduces ("grinds") the federal 35% refundable ITC base even if the corporation has no Ontario corporate income tax payable to absorb the ORDTC, a corporation may formally waive the ORDTC (or the OITC) in writing with its return within 6 months of its taxation year-end or on an amended return for that year12. Additionally, Ontario offers the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) on T2 Schedule 568, which provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred under eligible R&D contracts with qualifying Ontario research institutes (universities, colleges, and hospital research institutes), subject to an annual $20 million expenditure cap shared across an associated group (yielding a maximum $4 million credit)12.
6.2 Quebec: Transition from Legacy Form RD-1029.7 to the New CRIC Regime (2025–2026)

Quebec operates the most extensive autonomous R&D fiscal system in Canada, administered by Revenu Québec under the Taxation Act (Quebec)49. Auditors and claimants must carefully distinguish between taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025 and taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, as the Quebec 2025 Budget enacted a fundamental structural consolidation of all provincial R&D tax credits49.

For taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025, Quebec operated four separate refundable R&D credits: the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) claimed on Form RD-1029.7 (and Form RD-1029.7.8 for associated group allocations), the tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or research consortium, the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium, and the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research49. Under Form RD-1029.7, eligible Quebec R&D salaries and 50% of arm's-length Quebec subcontractor payments earned a base refundable rate of 14%, or an enhanced refundable rate of up to 30% on the first $3 million of eligible expenditures for corporations with worldwide assets under $50 million (phasing out linearly to 14% at $75 million in assets)49. Claims under RD-1029.7 were subject to a statutory exclusion threshold (a non-creditable deductible base starting at $50,000 for small corporations and scaling up to $225,000 as assets approached $75 million, allocated across eligible credits, with a $12,500 exclusion threshold rule applicable to qualified property in partnership contexts)51.

Effective for all taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, articles 1029.8.21.16.1 et seq. of the Quebec Taxation Act replaced all four legacy R&D credits (including the RD-1029.7 wage credit) with a single, harmonized Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation)32. The CRIC regime modernizes Quebec's incentive framework by establishing a unified two-tier refundable rate structure independent of corporate asset size: it provides a 30% fully refundable tax credit on the first $1 million of eligible expenditures above the applicable exclusion threshold, and a 20% fully refundable tax credit on all eligible expenditures exceeding that $1 million tier, applying to both SMEs and large corporations alike17. Furthermore, in addition to scientific R&D salaries and subcontractor costs, the CRIC expands the eligible expenditure base to encompass pre-commercialization activities (such as regulatory homologation, certification testing, industrial design, and late-stage commercialization validation that would otherwise be excluded under federal paragraph 248(1)(i)) as well as eligible R&D capital expenditures, aligning with the federal restoration of capital property while maintaining a streamlined exclusion threshold17. In addition, under Quebec's employee stock option rules in the Taxation Act, a corporation other than a CCPC qualifies for the enhanced security option deduction if the corporation was granted the CRIC (or one of the legacy R&D tax credits) for the taxation year or one of the three preceding taxation years and had total assets under $50 million49.
6.3 Western and Atlantic Provinces: Alberta IEG, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Regional Credits

Across Western and Atlantic Canada, provincial R&D incentives exhibit significant structural variation in rates, caps, and refundability12. In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)—codified in Sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and administered by the Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) pursuant to Information Circular IEG-1R5 and the Guide to Claiming the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant—applies to eligible R&D expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020 that match federal SR&ED eligibility12. The IEG provides a two-tier refundable payment on up to $4 million of annual Alberta R&D spending (producing a maximum annual benefit of up to $800,000): an 8% base payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's "base spending level" (computed as the average of the corporation's eligible Alberta R&D expenditures over the two immediately preceding taxation years), and an enhanced 20% incremental payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds the corporation's two-year base spending level12. The IEG phases out for corporations (and associated groups) with taxable capital employed in Canada between $10 million and $50 million, and claims are filed with the Alberta AT1 return using AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) and Form AT4970 (List of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Carried Out in Alberta) within 15 months after the corporation's AT1 filing due date (that is, 21 months after the taxation year-end, compared to 18 months federally)12.

In British Columbia, the BC SR&ED Tax Credit (Form T666), administered by the CRA, provides a 10% fully refundable tax credit to qualifying CCPCs with a permanent establishment in BC on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the CCPC's expenditure limit, and a 10% non-refundable tax credit (with a 10-year carryforward and 3-year carryback) to non-CCPCs and to CCPCs on expenditures exceeding their expenditure limit17. In Manitoba, the Manitoba Research and Development Tax Credit (Schedule 380) provides a 15% tax credit on eligible R&D expenditures incurred in Manitoba after April 11, 2017 (reduced from 20% prior to that date); for in-house R&D, one-half of the credit (7.5%) is refundable and the remaining 7.5% is non-refundable (carried back 3 years and forward 20 years), whereas R&D conducted in Manitoba under an eligible contract with a qualifying post-secondary educational institution is 100% refundable (full 15%)12. In Saskatchewan, CCPCs receive a 10% refundable credit on the first $1 million of eligible expenditures and a 10% non-refundable credit on additional expenditures and for non-CCPCs (subject to a combined $10 million annual cap), while Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Newfoundland and Labrador each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit to all corporations with a permanent establishment in the respective province without an expenditure limit ceiling, and Yukon provides a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit (expanded to 20% on payments to Yukon University).

body.text: 6.4 Government Assistance Stacking, the Federal Grind Formula, and NRC IRAP Integration

Under Paragraph 37(1)(d), Subsection 127(9), and Subsection 127(11.1) of the ITA, any provincial R&D tax credit, direct government grant, subsidy, or forgivable loan that a taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of SR&ED constitutes "government assistance"9. While the federal SR&ED ITC never reduces the eligible expenditure base of a provincial R&D tax credit, every dollar of provincial R&D tax credit or direct grant reduces ("grinds") the federal pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (Line 557 of Form T661) and the federal qualified SR&ED expenditures eligible for the federal ITC (Line 559 of Form T661)12.

Because of this statutory grind, federal and provincial R&D tax credit rates cannot simply be added together32. Instead, if a claimant's provincial credit rate is p and its federal ITC rate is f, the combined effective credit rate c on an eligible expenditure E (prior to proxy overhead multiplication) is governed by the multiplicative grind formula: c = p + f × (1 − p), so that the combined credit equals c × E.

The practical impact of the federal grind and the $3 million versus $6 million expenditure limit divergence in Ontario following Bill C-15 is illustrated by comparing a $500,000 claim against a full $6,000,000 claim for an Ontario CCPC that waives the non-refundable ORDTC12. On $500,000 of qualified current SR&ED expenditures in Ontario, the corporation first earns an 8% refundable Ontario OITC of $40,000; that $40,000 provincial credit grinds the federal qualified expenditure base down to $460,000, upon which the 35% federal enhanced ITC yields $161,000, resulting in a combined refundable recovery of $201,000 (an effective rate of 40.2%, rather than the $215,000 or 43.0% that naive addition would suggest)32. When that same Ontario CCPC scales its qualified current SR&ED expenditures to the full $6,000,000 federal limit enacted by Bill C-15, the first $3,000,000 band earns the maximum $240,000 Ontario OITC (grinding the federal base on that band to $2,760,000 and generating $966,000 in federal ITC, for a first-band subtotal of $1,206,000 at 40.2%), whereas the second $3,000,000 band (from $3.0 million to $6.0 million) exceeds Ontario's $3.0 million OITC cap, suffers zero provincial grind, and earns the full unground 35% federal enhanced ITC of $1,050,000—producing a total combined refundable credit of $2,256,000 (approximately $2.26 million, or a blended refundable rate of 37.6% across the $6 million spend)32.

body.text: Finally, claimants frequently stack retrospective SR&ED tax credits with prospective direct innovation grants—most notably the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) (which provides non-repayable contributions typically ranging from $50,000 to $500,000, with a median award of $75,000 and middle-half awards between $50,000 and $194,900, alongside its IP Assist sub-stream), Mitacs collaborative research internships (such as Mitacs AI Advantage), and provincial direct grants such as the Alberta Innovates Venture Development Grant (which replaced the legacy Alberta Innovates Micro Voucher and Voucher programs when they closed on May 29, 2026, providing $10,000 to $150,000 at up to 75% reimbursement for TRL 4–9 validation and technology development)19. When integrating NRC IRAP with SR&ED, claimants must navigate three structural rules3. First, NRC IRAP requires prospective application and pre-approval through an Industrial Technology Advisor (ITA) before eligible project costs are incurred, whereas SR&ED is claimed retrospectively on Form T66119. Second, although the NRC IRAP grant is deducted as government assistance in Part 3 and Part 4 of Form T661, under the Proxy Method the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 is calculated on the unreduced gross SR&ED salary base before the NRC IRAP grant is subtracted in Part 4, allowing a CCPC or ECPC to recover 70% to over 85% of its total cash R&D outlay across the combined grant and tax credit stack3. Third, unlike NRC IRAP (which grinds but stacks with SR&ED), provincial interactive digital media tax credits—such as the Ontario Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit (OIDMTC)—are strictly mutually exclusive with SR&ED at the labour level, prohibiting a taxpayer from claiming the same salary dollars for both OIDMTC and SR&ED19.
7. Strategic Compliance Synthesis and Audit Risk Mitigation

A rigorous technical and financial audit of Canadian R&D claims under the post-Bill C-15 statutory regime highlights seven interconnected compliance controls that corporate tax directors, chief financial officers, and engineering leads must enforce to maximize refundable recoveries while insulating claims against CRA and provincial reassessment5. First, corporate tax provision models and associated-group allocation agreements under Subsection 127(10.3) of the ITA for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 must be updated to reflect the enacted $6 million expenditure limit under Bill C-15 (generating up to $2.1 million in federal refundable credits) rather than the historical $3 million ceiling or the interim $4.5 million FES proposal, while newly eligible Canadian-resident public companies should be evaluated under the Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) average gross revenue phase-out rules ($15 million to $75 million) under Subsection 127(10.6) of the ITA1. Second, claimants must apply the exact 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) rate under Subsection 2900(4) of the ITR (never the obsolete pre-2013 65% rate) and perform an annual quantitative break-even analysis between the Proxy Method (Line 160) and the Traditional Method (Line 162), recognizing that cloud computing (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) and specialized software or CAD subscription invoices are strictly non-claimable under the Proxy Method and can only be claimed if the corporation elects the Traditional Method and tracks directly related, incremental usage8.

Third, payroll compliance systems must identify all specified employees (individuals owning 10% or more of any class of shares or dealing at non-arm's-length under subsection 248(1) of the ITA), strip out all bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and taxable benefits, cap direct SR&ED wages at $373,000.00 (5 × YMPE of $74,600 for 2026 under subsection 37(9.1) of the ITA), and cap their Part 5 proxy salary base inclusion at the lesser of 75% of base salary and $186,500.00 (2.5 × YMPE under subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the ITR)8. Fourth, for depreciable R&D equipment, tooling, moulds, and computers acquired after December 15, 2024, capital tracking ledgers must document the 90% "all or substantially all" (ASA) intended operating-time or value test (or the more-than-50% shared-use equipment test) to claim the restored federal deduction under paragraph 37(1)(b) and the 40%-refundable enhanced ITC under section 127.1, while systematically excluding those capital outlays from the Ontario OITC (Schedule 566) calculation, which remains restricted to current expenditures up to a $3 million cap1. Fifth, corporations with establishments in Quebec must transition their provincial compliance for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 from the legacy Form RD-1029.7 wage credit to the consolidated CRIC (30% on the first $1 million above the exclusion threshold; 20% above $1 million) regime, capturing newly eligible pre-commercialization validation, regulatory homologation, and capital expenditures17.

Sixth, in light of the Tax Court of Canada's ruling in National R&D Inc. v. The Queen (2020 TCC 65) and the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada (2026 FCA 175), engineering and scientific teams must structure their contemporaneous documentation (Git repositories, Jira tickets, laboratory notebooks, and test logs) so that it does not merely record coding tasks or hours worked, but explicitly captures the scientific or technological uncertainty (Line 242), the formulated hypothesis, the testing metrics demonstrating a logical progression between each test and preceding or subsequent tests (Line 244), and the resulting technological advancement (Line 246)5. Seventh, because Subsection 220(2.2) of the ITA strips the Minister of National Revenue and the courts of any discretion to waive or extend the statutory filing deadline under Subsection 37(11) and Paragraph 127(9)(m), claimants must enforce hard internal filing cut-offs well ahead of the 18-month post-year-end corporate deadline and verify that Part 9 of Form T661 (Claim preparer information) is accurately completed and signed on every return to prevent automatic $1,000 joint-and-several penalties under Subsection 162(5.1) of the ITA6.
